title: Automatic Construction of Clinical Scoring Systems with LLM Agents
claim: Existing ways of building compact decision rules rely on manual or post-hoc steps; ours automates rule construction with an LLM agent and verification loop.
layout: 3 columns, left-to-right: data, three methods stacked, resulting checklist and usage
description: A three-column flow read left to right, with big hollow arrows linking the columns. The left column, 'Clinical data', is a gray panel of icons: a clipboard form, a lab analyzer, a brain scan monitor, a t-SNE scatter plot, blood and urine samples, a histology slide with a microscope, a blood pressure cuff and an ECG trace. The middle column, 'Development methods', stacks three numbered boxes. (1) Manual curation shows experts at a table, then downstream validation, then a database. (2) Classical ML shows a database, then a sigmoid curve, then manual curation. (3) AgentScore shows a cycle of database, analysis tools, LLM agent, proposed rule and validation. The right column, 'Clinical scoring system', shows the CURB-65 checklist with green check marks and red crosses. Below it is a bedside usage panel: a clinician, a clipboard, a score of 3, and the outcomes of mortality risk and hospital admission.
caption: Clinical scoring systems: Clinical scoring systems translate routinely collected patient information into compact, explicit checklists that can be applied, recalled, and audited at the bedside. Traditional development relies on expert consensus, manual curation, or post-hoc simplification of classical machine-learning models. In contrast, AgentScore uses LLM-guided rule proposal together with deterministic, data-grounded validation to construct unit-weighted checklist scores.
abstract: Modern clinical practice relies on evidence-based guidelines implemented as compact scoring systems composed of a small number of interpretable decision rules. While machine-learning models achieve strong performance, many fail to translate into routine clinical use due to misalignment with workflow constraints such as memorability, auditability, and bedside execution. We argue that this gap arises not from insufficient predictive power, but from optimizing over model classes that are incompatible with guideline deployment. Deployable guidelines often take the form of unit-weighted clinical checklists, formed by thresholding the sum of binary rules, but learning such scores requires searching an exponentially large discrete space of possible rule sets. We introduce AgentScore, which performs semantically guided optimization in this space by using LLMs to propose candidate rules and a deterministic, data-grounded verification-and-selection loop to enforce statistical validity and deployability constraints. Across eight clinical prediction tasks, AgentScore outperforms existing score-generation methods and achieves AUROC comparable to more flexible interpretable models despite operating under stronger structural constraints. On two additional externally validated tasks, AgentScore achieves higher discrimination than established guideline-based scores.
